rationale:
Evidence: all three designs so far ended by off-track in all 60 trials. max_error sits at about 0.061 m every time, just past the 0.06 m limit (max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4) is 0.06 for every body width in range). rms_error is about 0.03 m whatever the gain. Halving the weights and changing kp, ki and kd moved progress only between 0.04 and 0.18, and iteration 2 (kp 2, ki 0.3, kd 0.8, base 1.3) was no better overall. The robot leaves the line at roughly the same point regardless of gain, so the common factor is speed (base 1.3 to 1.6) and the mismatch bias. At these speeds, the time the controller has to correct a bend is too short.

Changes (controller only, geometry held at iteration 2 so the result isolates the controller): (1) base_speed reduced from 1.3 to 0.9, to give the loop time to correct at each bend and cut lateral slip. (2) kp reduced from 2.0 to 1.2 to avoid the overshoot that the 1.3 to 1.6 runs suggest. (3) ki kept at 0.3 to cancel the constant left/right motor mismatch, with the integral bounded at +/-2. (4) kd kept at 0.8 to damp the response at the lower gain. (5) line_loss kept at last_direction. The earlier loss events were few, so changing this is not justified by the evidence.

Trade-off: at 0.9 base speed the robot is unlikely to finish within 3 s, so the 500-point completion bonus is probably out of reach this iteration. Progress is worth up to 250 points plus a middle term, so a stable run that covers most of the course is the priority. Expected result: no early off-track exit, max_error below about 0.05 m, and progress well above 0.5 on the development tracks. If the run is still stable and slow, the next step is to raise base_speed toward 1.2 while keeping kp near 1.2.
